title: Origin and Reduction of Coercive Fields in ZnO-based Wurtzite Ferroelectrics
authors: Abhijeet Dhakane, Alireza Sepehrinezhad, William Prudnick, Jon-Paul Maria, Bobby Sumpter, Adri C. T. van Duin, Kyle P. Kelley, P. Ganesh
abstract: Wurtzite ferroelectrics offer a route to semiconductor-compatible non-volatile devices, but their large coercive fields (E$_c$) constrain the operating window between polarization reversal, leakage and dielectric breakdown. Atomically localized and non-classical switching fronts have recently been identified in wurtzite nitrides, yet the microscopic feature that sets the coercive field remains unresolved. Here we use large-scale reactive molecular dynamics, parameterized against first-principles data, to follow field-driven reversal in pristine, Mg-modified and heterostructured ZnO. Reversal proceeds through rugged inversion-boundary filaments in agreement with recent observations in other wurtzite ferroelectrics. We find that the field required for switching is controlled by the advancing filament head, which is a under-coordinated reconstructed inversion-boundary region during the transient switching dynamics with a large field-aligned local polar-order amplitude that is only partially compensated by an oppositely oriented surrounding shell. Controlled strain-only and charge-doping-only perturbations show that charge redistribution lowers the coercive field more effectively than strain because it suppresses this field-setting unscreened local polar order at the filament head, with the combined effect lowering E$_c$ by $\sim$ 50 \%. Layered ZnO/ZnMgO architectures further create buried nucleation sites and shorten filament propagation lengths. These results connect atomistic switching topology to a materials-design principle for substantially reducing coercive fields in ZnO-based wurtzite ferroelectrics.
summary: This work uses reactive molecular dynamics to investigate why wurtzite ferroelectrics have high coercive fields. The research identifies that the field is set by the local polarization required at the advancing switching filament head. By showing that charge doping is more effective than strain in reducing this local barrier, the authors propose a materials design principle for creating low-field ferroelectric devices.
main_problem: The large coercive fields in wurtzite ferroelectrics limit their operational window for non-volatile memory devices, and the microscopic origin of this field remains unresolved.
main_result: The coercive field is determined by the local polar-order amplitude required to advance the reconstructed inversion-boundary filament head, and charge redistribution is a more effective way to lower this field than strain alone.
method: The study uses large-scale reactive molecular dynamics, parameterized against first-principles data, to simulate field-driven polarization reversal.
model_or_system: The system is ZnO-based wurtzite ferroelectrics, studied in pristine, Mg-modified, and heterostructured (ZnO/ZnMgO) forms. The simulation tracks the dynamics of polarization reversal through inversion-boundary filaments.
key_observables: Hysteresis loops, local polar-order vectors, the advancing filament head polarization ($P_{	ext{fil-head}}$), and the polarization imbalance ($\Delta$).
important_parameters: Coercive field ($E_c$), applied electric field, strain magnitude, and charge doping concentration.
main_assumptions: The switching mechanism is governed by the advancement of a specific, under-coordinated, reconstructed inversion-boundary region.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the polarization-field response, the evolution of inversion-boundary filaments, the core-shell structure of the switching front, and the dependence of $E_c$ on local polarization imbalance ($\Delta$) for different perturbations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (high $E_c$), develops the mechanism (filament advancement controlled by the head), compares perturbations (charge vs. strain), and proposes a design principle using heterostructures to engineer lower switching fields.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state ferroelectrics, the study's detailed atomistic simulation of non-equilibrium phase transitions, domain wall dynamics, and field-induced structural reconstruction provides valuable insights into complex many-body dynamics far from equilibrium.
